ta-l1d42q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinctions 42–44 on God's power. Lombard first shows its universality, by which God is called omnipotent, and then (Dist. 43) excludes the error of those who limit it. He asks why God is called omnipotent and determines that he can do all things, by many authorities, excluding three instances (bodily acts, sins, passions) that we can do and he cannot, and concluding the complete character of omnipotence; then he treats authorities saying he is omnipotent because he can do whatever he wills, answers them, and distinguishes senses of 'he can do whatever he wills' so it is proper to God. Thomas asks about God's power in itself and about what falls under it. On the first, whether power belongs to God, and whether there is one power in him or several.
claims: God is omnipotent because he can do all things, not merely whatever he wills.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e131.summary: First argument that power does not belong to God. As power relates to act, the first act relates to power, and the first power, matter, has no act in its essence, so the first act, God, has no power.
claims: First act excludes potency.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e134.summary: Second argument. What acts not by its essence acts through some power, power being midway between essence and operation, but God acts by his essence (Dionysius, Avicenna).
claims: God acts by his essence, not by a power.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e137.summary: Third argument. Power is active or passive. God has no passive power, being impassible, nor active power, which is the principle of change in another as other (the Philosopher), since God requires no matter to act on.
claims: Active power requires matter to act on.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e141.summary: Fourth argument. Every power is principle of an operation, and God's only operation is his essence, which has no principle, being neither begotten nor proceeding.
claims: God's operation has no principle.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e144.summary: Fifth argument. God's power is either always joined to act, and then its effects, creatures, would be eternal, which is heretical, or not, and then it is imperfect, perfected by act.
claims: Power joined to act yields eternal effects; unjoined it is imperfect.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e147.summary: Sed contra from Luke 1:49, 'he who is mighty has done great things for me', and Ps. 88:9, 'you are mighty, Lord'.
claims: Scripture calls God mighty.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e156.summary: Second sed contra. Every effect is produced by the power of its efficient cause, and God is the efficient cause of things.
claims: Efficient causes have power.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e159.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Power' was first imposed to signify human power, as we call some people powerful (Avicenna), and then transferred to natural things. Among humans he is powerful who can do what he wills with others without impediment, and his power diminishes as he can be impeded, which happens to natural and voluntary agents insofar as they can be acted on. So by its first imposition the concept of power includes not being able to suffer, so even what cannot suffer, though it can do nothing, is called powerful, as the hard has the power not to be cut. Hence the complete character of power is in God, both because he acts on all things, as first and perfect act (nothing acts except as in act), and because he suffers nothing, as pure act without matter, since things suffer by something material in them.
claims: Power by its first meaning is acting without being impeded or acted upon, perfectly in God as pure act.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e162.summary: Reply to the first argument. Being first power does not belong to matter in the principal sense of power, which was first imposed for the principle of action and then transferred to what receives the agent's action, passive power; as operation corresponds to active power, completing it, what corresponds to passive power as its perfection is called act. So every form is called act, even separate forms, and the principle of all perfection, God, is called first and pure act, to whom that active power most belongs.
claims: Active power belongs most to pure act; passive power is a derived sense.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e166.summary: Reply to the second argument. Power implies the character of principle of action, so whatever is a principle of acting is called a power, like heat and cold, and the divine essence, as principle of operation, is called power, not as though power differed from essence in God.
claims: God's power is his essence as principle of operation.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e169.summary: Reply to the third argument. God has no passive power, only active. That active power requires subject matter to act on is incidental, belonging to imperfect power not reaching the whole substance of a thing, which is removed from divine power. Or, according to Avicenna, an agent is said differently in natural and divine things: natural agents act by motion, which requires matter, being the act of what is in potency, while the divine agent acts by giving being, not by motion, so active power is a principle of operation in another as in a produced effect, not as in transformed matter.
claims: Divine active power needs no matter, giving being without motion.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e172.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. God does not act by an intermediate operation other than his essence; his being is his operating and his operating his essence. Still, the essence is signified as principle of being, and likewise power can be signified as principle of operating and also of what is produced.
claims: Power is signified as principle of operation and of the operated.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e175.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. His operation is really the same as his power, so his power cannot fail to be joined to operation. But the effect does not always follow whenever the operation is, since the operation is in a way regulated by ordering will and wisdom, so the effect follows only at the nod of the divine will, by whose disposition a temporal effect follows from eternal operation.
claims: Eternal operation yields temporal effects by the disposition of will.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e187.summary: First argument that there is not only one power in God. The same cannot be proper to one and common to several, and the power to create is common to the three while the power to beget is proper to the Father.
claims: Power to beget is proper, power to create common.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e190.summary: Second argument. In us natural acts (generating), voluntary acts (building), and animal acts (understanding) reduce to different powers, and similar acts correspond in God (knowing, creating, begetting), so there are several powers in him.
claims: Different acts, different powers.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e193.summary: Third argument. According to philosophers, separate substances divide into intellect and will, not as different natures, so as different powers, so God has at least two powers.
claims: Intellect and will are different powers.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e197.summary: Fourth argument. Power is a principle of operation, and every divine attribute by its own concept is a principle of operation (from his goodness all goodness, from his life all life, Dionysius), so as there are several attributes there are several powers.
claims: Each attribute is a principle.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e200.summary: Sed contra. Whatever is said absolutely of God is predicated singularly (Augustine), and power is absolute.
claims: Absolute names are singular.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e203.summary: Second sed contra. Every united power is more infinite than a multiplied one (Liber de causis), and divine power is most infinite, so most one.
claims: United power is more infinite.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e206.summary: Thomas's determination. Simply and absolutely there is only one power in God. Since power, in our mode of understanding, is between essence and operation, its unity and diversity can be weighed from either side, but simply it has unity and multiplication from the side of the essence, not the essence as its subject, since one essence can have several powers, but as the immediate principle of the act, as in fire lightness is the power to move upward and heat the power to burn. From the side of operation a power is called one or many not simply but in some respect, rather one power of many than many powers. Since the immediate principle of every divine operation is his essence, which is simply one, his power is one; but as principle of conceptually distinct operations it takes different concepts of power, as the essence has several concepts of attributes, without being several. Active power, the only kind in God, can be considered as to its essence, the immediate principle of the act (as heat of heating), and as to the actions proceeding from it. The principle of all divine operations is his essence, by which he acts, so as his essence is one in reality with a plurality of concepts by the attributes (Dist. 2), his power is one in reality with a plurality of concepts, since the character of power belongs to each attribute as principle of operation. His operation, being his essence, is one in reality, signified variously by the attributes and by the diversity of effects, which are simply many. So the power, whether considered in its essence or in relation to operation as in the operator, is one, and real multitude is only in the effects. So absolutely divine power is one but of many, since unity is judged absolutely by a thing's essence, not by what is outside.
claims: There is one power in God, since its immediate principle, his essence, is one; it has many concepts by the attributes and many effects.
Unity of power is judged by its principle, not by its effects.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e209.summary: Reply to the first argument. The generative power names the essential joined to the notional, as 'God begets', so what is essential to the concept of power is common to the three, like the power of being, since by the same power the Father begets and the Son is born, but the notion remains proper to the Father (Dist. 26).
claims: Generative power is the essence with a notion; the power is common, the notion proper.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e212.summary: Reply to the second argument. In God the principle of being and of operating is the same, so as God is one, being, and just by the same, he performs acts of different concepts by the same, while we do so by different powers.
claims: God acts in many ways by one principle.
concepts: one principle of being and acting

ta-l1d42q1-d1e216.summary: Reply to the third argument. In other separate substances will and intellect seem not wholly the same in reality, but what in them is by real diversity is in God by unity of reality and distinction of concept.
claims: Intellect and will are one in God, distinct in creatures.

ta-l1d42q1-d1e219.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The attributes are one in reality and distinct only conceptually, so 'power', and any first-imposition name of a thing, cannot be predicated plurally ('several attributes are several powers', 'several goodnesses'), but second-imposition names like 'attribute' are predicated plurally.
claims: First-imposition names are singular in God; second-imposition names can be plural.

ta-l1d42q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 42 divides Lombard's treatment of divine omnipotence, its universality and the exclusion of errors limiting it, and announces two questions, the first with articles on whether power belongs to God and whether it is one.
claims: God is omnipotent because he can do all things.

ta-l1d42q1-Dd1e123.summary: Article 1 holds that power belongs to God in its first, fullest sense, acting without being impeded or acted upon, since he is pure act. Active power belongs most to pure act, and God's power is his essence as principle of operation. It needs no matter, giving being without motion, and his eternal operation yields temporal effects by the disposition of his will.
claims: God has perfect active power as pure act, identical with his essence.

ta-l1d42q1-Dd1e179.summary: Article 2 holds that there is simply one power in God, since unity of power is judged by its immediate principle, his one essence, though it has many concepts by the attributes and many effects. Generative power is the essence with a notion, intellect and will are one in God, and first-imposition names like 'power' are not pluralized.
claims: Divine power is one, of many effects.

ta-l1d42q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 42 treats God's power in itself. Article 1 holds that power belongs to God most perfectly, as pure act who acts on all and is acted on by nothing, his power being his essence as principle of operation, needing no matter. Article 2 holds that his power is one, its principle being his one essence, conceptually many by the attributes and really many only in its effects.
claims: God's power is his essence as principle of operation.
Divine power is one, really many only in effects.
